Scrutinize

SKROO-tuh-nyze · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To scrutinize is to examine something closely and thoroughly, often with a critical or suspicious eye.

Before hiring the new babysitter, the parents scrutinized every one of her references, calling each family personally.

Worked Example

Before submitting their results, the research team scrutinized every data point one final time, looking for even the smallest error.

Scrutinizing means going over every detail carefully, often specifically looking for a mistake, flaw, or hidden problem.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

inspect: to examine closely, especially for flaws

examine: to look over something closely

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

ignore: to pay no attention to something

neglect: to fail to give something the attention it needs

Where it sits · how fierce the examination gets — review → scrutinize → interrogate

review vs. scrutinize: To review something is to look it over generally, far less intense than scrutinizing every detail.

interrogate vs. scrutinize: To interrogate someone is to question them intensely and often aggressively, a more forceful act than simply scrutinizing their story.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — scrutin

root — scrutin: to search thoroughly (Latin scrutari)

suffix — -ize

suffix — -ize: to perform an action, to make (Greek -izein)

Put it together

Put it together: Scrutinize comes from Latin scrutari ('to search thoroughly,' originally 'to rummage through trash looking for something') + -ize ('to perform an action') -- which is exactly what scrutinizing means: searching through every detail as if nothing could be missed.

Use the root in a new word: scrutiny

Use the root in a new word: scrutiny: The mayor's spending came under intense scrutiny after the leaked documents surfaced.

Root Check

Word Choice

Scrutinize can apply to anything -- documents, behavior, motives, data -- and usually implies suspicion or a search for flaws. Peruse, by contrast, is limited to reading text closely, and doesn't necessarily imply any distrust at all.
